claim: Most computer interaction uses gestures and natural speech
originalWording: Most computer interaction uses gestures and natural speech

sources.title: The Age of Spiritual Machines — Ray Kurzweil (1999)
sources.locator: Computers and communications in 2019: keyboards and interaction

sourceCaveat: The original book edition has not been independently checked. See the listed source on Sources for attribution limits.

strict.criterion: Gestures and natural spoken interaction predominate and keyboards become rare, retaining the substantive keyboard-rarity clause.
strict.rationale: Touchscreens and assistants were widespread by 2019, but keyboards remained normal. Multimodal AI expands the predicted interface, yet physical and on-screen keyboards are not rare. The compound remains partial.

evidence.title: Apple launches iPhone 4S, iOS 5 and iCloud
evidence.note: Announcement; retail availability October 14. This is NOT the first-ever voice assistant, nor the first standalone Siri release.

evidence.title: Gartner: Worldwide smartphone sales in 2013
evidence.note: 968 million smartphones; Android plus iOS dominated. Inferring physical-keyboard-free portable computing requires a population definition, not simply counting all feature phones.

evidence.title: Microsoft Teams reaches 13 million daily active users
evidence.note: Primary institutional, research, or issuer source. Dates in the claim refer to the observation or product event, not the review date.

broader.criterion: Spoken language and touch/gesture interaction become major everyday input modes alongside keyboards.
broader.rationale: Touch gestures and voice assistants are ordinary everyday interfaces, earning solid partial credit. Even charitably, however, typing on physical laptop keyboards and virtual phone keyboards remains central to computing rather than rare.
changedConditions: Credits widespread touch and voice input as partial without erasing the keyboard-rarity claim
